RagShortTexts: A treaty and its consequences belong to the uncertain future, not current fact.
Michael Palaiologos has not exchanged Galata concessions for a fleet.

Variants.Content: In 1259 Nicaea still seeks a way to recover Constantinople from the Latin Empire, and control of the sea is central to that ambition. Genoa and Venice compete for trade and influence, giving Michael Palaiologos reason to sound out potential naval partners. Yet no Treaty of Nymphaeum has been concluded, and Genoa has not received the later privileges at Galata or the Black Sea. Negotiators may discuss ships, customs exemptions and commercial quarters, but each concession would require bargaining and could provoke rivals. Nicaean officials must weigh the immediate value of galleys against long-term revenue and political dependence. A treaty and its consequences belong to the uncertain future, not current fact.

A Nicaean notable may argue Genoese ships could isolate Latin-held Constantinople; rivals fear lost customs income. Michael Palaiologos has not exchanged Galata concessions for a fleet. Proposals must specify ships, tolls and legal rights. Lords debate alliance costs rather than celebrate a bargain already made.

A Nicaean sailor may hear Genoese captains are open to bargaining, but no treaty fleet is summoned and no squadron is pledged against Venice. Patrols watch merchants and carry messages between forts. A commander checks stores and awaits orders. Italian ships may be allies, rivals or neutral traders; a soldier cannot treat a future pact as a standing battle plan.

A Greek coastal household in 1259 may hope that Nicaea can find ships and allies against Latin sea power. Italian merchants offer trade while seeking favourable terms for themselves. The pact later concluded at Nymphaeum has not yet been signed, so a boatman cannot describe its privileges or military consequences as events already transforming the shore.
